name: Flavoured Pink Gin
description: Gin sweetened and coloured with red fruit — strawberry, raspberry, rhubarb — which took over British gin shelves in the late 2010s. Legally often not gin at all but a gin-based spirit drink, because of the sugar.
funFact: EU rules cap sweetening in anything sold as gin, so most pink gins are legally classed as gin-based spirit drinks rather than gin.

serve.glass: Chilled coupe for the classic, copa for the modern
serve.how: With tonic and ice, or with sparkling wine. It is sweet enough that a dry tonic and a wedge of lemon rather than more fruit keeps it in balance. Not to be confused with the naval Pink Gin, which is a cocktail of gin and Angostura and tastes nothing like this.

composition.summary: Gin sweetened and flavoured with red fruit after distillation.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Strawberry, raspberry, redcurrant or rhubarb, plus sugar

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Fruit infused after distillation, not redistilled

composition.process: Sugar above 0.1g per litre disqualifies it from the plain gin designation in the EU.

name: Cream Gin
description: A Victorian curiosity revived by modern bartenders: gin redistilled with dairy cream, which leaves the texture and the sweetness behind but not the fat. Silky, faintly lactic, and entirely clear.
funFact: Nineteenth-century gin palaces sold it from casks, and the recipe was reconstructed in the 2000s from a Victorian bartending manual.

serve.how: In a Martini variant or a Ramos-style fizz, where the texture does work no other gin can. It is clear in the glass, so the mouthfeel takes people by surprise.

composition.summary: Gin redistilled with dairy cream so texture carries but fat does not.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Cream added to the still and the spirit redistilled off it

composition.process: Distilling off the cream captures lactones and sugars while leaving fat and solids in the pot.

name: Gin de Mahón
description: Menorca's protected gin, distilled in wood-fired copper stills from wine alcohol rather than grain — a legacy of the British occupation of the island in the eighteenth century.
funFact: The British held Menorca for most of the 1700s and the Royal Navy's demand for gin outlived the occupation by three centuries.

serve.how: As a pomada — gin with cloudy lemonade over ice, which is the island's summer drink and served by the jug at the Sant Joan festival. Neat it is softer and rounder than a grain-based gin.

composition.summary: Wine alcohol redistilled with juniper over a wood fire.

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper dominant, with a short supporting list

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills over wood fires

composition.process: A wine base gives a rounder, slightly fruitier body than neutral grain spirit.

name: Jonge Jenever
description: The young style, capped at 15% malt wine, developed in the 1950s when grain was scarce and drinkers wanted something lighter. Closer to a soft vodka with a whisper of juniper than to gin.
funFact: Young and old here refer to the recipe rather than to ageing — a jonge jenever can be older in cask than an oude one.

serve.glass: Small tulip, filled to the brim
serve.how: From the freezer, poured until it domes over the rim, first sip taken with hands behind the back. A blonde lager alongside makes it a kopstootje — a headbutt.

composition.summary: Neutral grain spirit with a small proportion of malt wine and juniper.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral grain spirit, max 15% malt wine

composition.process: Wartime grain shortages drove the style, and Dutch taste never went back.

name: Oude Jenever
description: The old style, requiring at least 15% malt wine and often carrying far more. Maltier, rounder and closer to what gin tasted like in the seventeenth century before the English stripped the grain out of it.
funFact: English soldiers fighting in the Low Countries brought the habit home, and the phrase Dutch courage dates from those campaigns.

serve.how: Cold and neat, or in a Holland Gin cocktail from a pre-Prohibition book — those recipes were written for this, not for London Dry, and taste entirely different when made correctly.

composition.summary: Malt wine and neutral spirit blended with juniper, often cask-rested.

components.label: Base
components.detail: At least 15% malt wine from rye, corn and malted barley

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper, sometimes with caraway and aniseed

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot-distilled malt wine plus redistilled botanicals

composition.process: The malt wine is the flavour; juniper is seasoning rather than the point.

name: Mediterranean Gin
description: A Spanish-led style built on olive, rosemary, thyme and citrus rather than a juniper spine, and served in enormous balloon glasses packed with ice. It changed how the whole world serves gin and tonic.
funFact: The oversized copa de balón came from Basque chefs, who reasoned that a wider bowl and more ice kept the drink colder and released more aroma.

serve.glass: Copa de balón, filled with ice
serve.how: Fill the glass with ice, add gin, then tonic poured down a bar spoon. Garnish to match the botanicals — rosemary, a strip of grapefruit, a green olive. Not lime, which fights the herbs.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit redistilled with Mediterranean botanicals and softer juniper.

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Arbequina olive, rosemary, thyme, basil, citrus peel, juniper

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, often with separate botanical distillates blended

composition.process: Pulling juniper back to make room for herbs is what defines the style and irritates traditionalists.

name: German Gin
description: Germany's gin scene grew out of its fruit-brandy tradition, so the base spirit is often grape or fruit rather than grain. Black Forest botanicals — spruce, lavender, angelica — dominate.
funFact: Monkey 47 takes its name from 47 botanicals and 47% ABV, and was inspired by a Black Forest recipe left by a British RAF officer after the war.

serve.how: With a light tonic and a garnish that echoes the forest — a spruce tip, a slice of apple, or lingonberries. Heavy Mediterranean tonics bury the delicate lavender and spruce entirely.

composition.summary: Grain or fruit spirit redistilled with Black Forest botanicals.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral grain, or a molasses and fruit blend

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper, spruce, lavender, lingonberry, angelica, bramble leaf

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Small copper pot stills, often fruit-brandy equipment

composition.process: A fruit-distilling heritage means German gin makers think about maceration times differently than grain distillers.

name: French Gin
description: Frequently built on a grape base rather than grain, which gives a softer, rounder body. Distillers borrow from perfumery and from wine, using floral botanicals and sometimes finishing in wine casks.
funFact: Grape-based gin is legal and increasingly common — the EU sets no restriction on the source of the neutral alcohol, only on the juniper.

serve.how: With a neutral tonic and a strip of lemon or a sprig of thyme. The grape base makes it unusually good in a Martini, where its softness reads as texture rather than weakness.

composition.summary: Grape or grain spirit redistilled with floral botanicals.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grape spirit, often from Cognac or the Loire

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper, rose, iris root, citrus blossom, cubeb

composition.process: Grape spirit carries more body than grain, so French gin often needs less sweetening to taste round.

name: Nordic Gin
description: Built on foraged Scandinavian botanicals — dill, caraway, lingonberry, sea buckthorn, birch — and sometimes on aquavit's spice palette. Clean, herbal and unmistakably northern.
funFact: Juniper grows wild across all of Scandinavia and has flavoured Nordic food and drink for centuries, long before anyone there made gin.

serve.how: With a dry tonic and a sprig of dill or a few lingonberries. The caraway note means it also works in a Martini for anyone who likes aquavit — it sits halfway between the two categories.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit redistilled with foraged Nordic botanicals.

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper, dill, caraway, lingonberry, sea buckthorn, birch, meadowsweet

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, often with vapour baskets

composition.process: Wild-foraged botanicals mean batches shift with the season, which producers treat as a feature.

name: Mexican Gin
description: Gin distilled with Mexican botanicals — damiana, cempasúchil marigold, avocado leaf, guava — and often on a base of agave or cane spirit rather than grain. A young category with a distinct accent.
funFact: Cempasúchil, the marigold used on Day of the Dead altars, appears in several Mexican gins and gives a distinctly resinous, floral note.

serve.how: With tonic and a slice of grapefruit or a sprig of epazote. The agave-based versions carry a vegetal edge that makes them excellent in a Negroni against a bitter amaro.

composition.summary: Agave, cane or grain spirit redistilled with Mexican botanicals.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Agave, cane or neutral grain spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper, damiana, cempasúchil, avocado leaf, guava, lime

composition.process: An agave base is what marks the most distinctive Mexican gins out from imports.

name: Bathtub Gin
description: Compound gin — botanicals steeped in finished spirit rather than redistilled — which is how gin was made illicitly during Prohibition and legitimately for centuries before. Cloudier, softer and fuller than a distilled gin.
funFact: The name comes from the story that Prohibition-era producers topped their bottles with water from a bathtub tap, being too tall to fit under a sink.

serve.how: With tonic and orange rather than lime — the cold-compounding leaves a rounder, spicier gin that suits a warmer garnish. It also makes an unusually rich Negroni.

composition.summary: Botanicals steeped directly in finished spirit and filtered, not redistilled.

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper, orange peel, coriander, cassia, cardamom, clove

composition.process: Infusing rather than redistilling carries colour and oils that a still would leave behind.

name: Damson Gin
description: Damsons steeped in gin with sugar, the darker and tarter cousin of sloe gin. An English hedgerow tradition made at home each autumn and drunk the following winter.
funFact: Damsons were once grown in vast numbers in Westmorland for dyeing cloth as much as for eating, and the surviving orchards now supply gin makers.

serve.how: Neat after dinner, or topped with sparkling wine. Tarter than sloe gin and less almond-driven, and it makes an excellent substitute in a Sloe Gin Fizz for anyone who finds sloe too sweet.

composition.summary: Damsons steeped in gin with sugar for several months.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Damsons, sugar; stones often left in

composition.process: Stones left in the steep supply the almond note, exactly as in sloe gin.

name: Rye Vodka
description: The Polish classic, distilled from rye and left with more character than the wheat and potato styles. Peppery, faintly spicy and sweeter on the finish than most drinkers expect vodka to be.
funFact: Rye was the grain of choice across Poland long before wheat, because it tolerates the poor sandy soils that wheat will not grow in.

serve.how: Cold rather than frozen — freezer temperatures mute exactly the peppery character that makes rye vodka worth choosing. With food, in small measures, alongside herring or salo.

composition.summary: Rye fermented and rectified, then cut with water.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column rectification, though not to full neutrality in good examples

composition.process: Stopping rectification slightly short is what leaves the grain character in the glass.

name: Wheat Vodka
description: The lightest and sweetest of the grain vodkas, and the base for most premium Western brands. Soft, faintly aniseed and easy — which is exactly why it dominates the market.
funFact: Wheat's high starch and low protein make it the most efficient grain for producing neutral spirit, which is as much of the reason for its dominance as taste.

serve.glass: Chilled shot glass, or Martini glass
serve.how: From the freezer, neat, or as the base of a Martini where its softness lets vermouth show. It is the least assertive vodka style, which makes it the safest in any mixed drink.

composition.summary: Winter wheat fermented and heavily rectified.
composition.process: Charcoal filtration after distillation removes what little congener content survives.

name: Grape Vodka
description: Distilled from wine grapes rather than grain, which produces a vodka with noticeable floral and stone-fruit character. Naturally gluten-free, and a French speciality built on the country's wine surplus.
funFact: France produces more wine than it drinks, and distilling the surplus is a centuries-old solution that vodka gave a new market to.

serve.how: Cold and neat, or in a Martini where the fruit character is a genuine asset. It is silkier than grain vodka and worth trying beside one to see how much the base material survives rectification.

composition.summary: Wine grapes fermented and rectified into neutral spirit.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Wine grapes, often Ugni Blanc or Colombard

composition.process: Even at high rectification a trace of the grape's terpenes carries into the finished spirit.

name: Whey Vodka
description: Distilled from the whey left over from cheesemaking, fermenting its lactose into alcohol. A genuinely circular use of a waste stream, and produced seriously in New Zealand and Ireland.
funFact: Cheese whey was for decades a disposal problem for dairies; fermenting its lactose turned a pollutant into a premium spirit.

serve.how: Cold and neat, or in a Martini. It carries a faint creaminess that survives rectification, which makes it noticeably rounder than grain vodka in a stirred drink.

composition.summary: Cheese whey fermented on its lactose and rectified.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Whey from cheddar or similar cheesemaking

composition.process: Lactose needs specific yeast strains to ferment, which is the technical hurdle the category had to clear.

name: Khrenovukha
description: Vodka infused with horseradish, honey and sometimes lemon, and one of Russia's most enduring household infusions. Sharp, hot and genuinely sinus-clearing, drunk with heavy food in winter.
funFact: Peter the Great is credited with decreeing that vodka be infused with horseradish, though the story is repeated far more often than it is sourced.

serve.how: Straight from the freezer, in one, with fatty food. The cold blunts the horseradish just enough to make it possible; at room temperature it is close to unpleasant.

composition.summary: Vodka infused with fresh horseradish root and honey.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Fresh horseradish root, honey, sometimes lemon and mustard seed

composition.process: Steeping time is critical — left too long the horseradish turns bitter and overwhelming.

name: Wiśniówka
description: Polish cherry-infused vodka, made at home each summer by steeping sour cherries with sugar. Deep red, sweet-tart, and one of the most widely made nalewki in the country.
funFact: The steeped cherries are eaten afterwards and are, by that point, considerably more alcoholic than the drink itself.

serve.how: At cellar temperature after a meal, with a couple of the steeped cherries in the glass. Polish households open the summer's batch at Christmas, which is when it is at its best.

composition.summary: Sour cherries macerated in vodka with sugar for months.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Sour cherries, sugar; some stones left in

composition.process: Cracked stones supply the almond note that separates a good wiśniówka from cherry syrup.

name: Citron Vodka
description: Lemon-flavoured vodka, launched in 1988 and responsible almost single-handedly for the Cosmopolitan and the Lemon Drop. The flavoured-vodka boom of the 1990s started here.
funFact: Absolut Citron's launch is generally credited with kicking off the flavoured vodka category, which grew to hundreds of variants within a decade.

serve.how: In a Cosmopolitan or a Lemon Drop, both of which were built around it. Neat from the freezer it is sharper and cleaner than the sugary flavoured vodkas that followed it.

composition.summary: Grain vodka flavoured with citrus peel distillate.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Citrus distillate blended in after rectification

composition.process: Better versions use a peel distillate rather than an essence, and the difference is obvious neat.

name: Swedish Vodka
description: Made from winter wheat grown on the plains around Åhus and distilled continuously rather than in batches. Soft, faintly grainy and the template most premium Western vodka followed.
funFact: Absolut is distilled entirely in one small Swedish town, using wheat grown within a short radius and water from a local well — a level of concentration unusual at that scale.

serve.glass: Chilled shot glass or Martini glass
serve.how: Freezer cold and neat with food, in the Swedish snaps tradition, or as a clean Martini base. Its softness makes it forgiving in almost any mixed drink.

composition.summary: Winter wheat continuously distilled and cut with local water.
composition.process: Continuous rather than batch distillation is what gives the consistency the brand was built on.

name: Birch Sap Vodka
description: Made using birch sap, tapped from trees for a few weeks each spring as the ground thaws. Faintly sweet and mineral, and a Baltic and Nordic tradition older than vodka itself.
funFact: Birch sap runs for only two or three weeks a year, and a mature tree yields just a few litres a day before the leaves open and the flow stops.

serve.how: Cold and neat in a small glass. The sap character is delicate, so it is wasted in a mixed drink — this is one to taste beside a plain grain vodka to see what the sap actually does.

composition.summary: Grain spirit cut or fermented with spring-tapped birch sap.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grain spirit, with birch sap in place of water or in the ferment

composition.process: The harvest window is fixed by the thaw, so annual production is capped by nature rather than demand.

name: Quinoa Vodka
description: Distilled from Andean quinoa, a seed rather than a grain, giving a naturally gluten-free spirit with a distinctly nutty character. A modern South American answer to the premium vodka market.
funFact: Quinoa must be washed thoroughly before use because its natural saponin coating is bitter and soapy — a step that matters as much for distilling as for cooking.

serve.how: Cold and neat, or in a Martini where the nuttiness gives more to work with than grain vodka does. It also stands up well in a savoury cocktail.

composition.summary: Andean quinoa fermented and rectified into vodka.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Royal quinoa from the Bolivian altiplano

composition.process: Saponins must be washed off before fermentation or they carry a bitterness right through the process.
